Marie Bradley  

This is a book which I found at first curiously difficult to read, hence the writing of this review has spanned a considerable time. On reflection I think this had something to do with the author's powerful evocation of living with, and being in touch with, the children who are often our patients.

Divided into two parts, the first -‘Making love’ - describes the author and her family's experience of fostering twelve young people, over a period of twenty-five years. It is, as she says, ‘an experience of family life with children who have lived through overwhelming stress’. Sometimes inspiring, at times despairing, it is a raw, impressive and touching account. What she describes is a family - with a difference - living in the community. All of their foster children have stayed in touch through the years. As Cairns says, this is not a ‘how to do it’ book, but a story; she tells the story in an accessible way which cannot fail to be painful to hear, but manages to convey hopefulness too.

In this first section, Cairns begins to address the issues which will form the substantive part of the second section. These are attachment, trauma and resilience. Drawing on particular experiences with individual children, she has formed ‘composites’ of her twelve fostered children. From these she talks about ordinary, good-enough emotional development in relation to attachment, trauma and resilience, and about what it means for development when such ordinary experiences are absent. She describes how the absence of good early infantile experiences can mean the lack of the relational skills we ordinarily take for granted; how trust, fun and playfulness, curiosity and interest in the world may then be missing, further depriving the child of new developmental opportunities.

Her theoretical thinking about children in this predicament, and their responses to the demands and possibilities of new relationships proceeds from this emotional understanding and experience of unmet and disrupted attachments.

Winnicott was an avid reader of biographies. Or rather, he was an avid reader of the first few chapters of biographies, those dealing with the subject's childhood and adolescence. The rest could be taken as read. Faced, therefore, with this new full-length biography of Winnicott, one is tempted to wonder what he himself might have made of its early pages. For one thing Rodman's account starts not at the

120

beginning of his life, nor at the end, where Winnicott chose to begin his own brief, incomplete autobiography. Instead he introduces us to Winnicott the fully-fledged psychoanalyst at nearly fifty addressing a scientific meeting of his fellows in 1945 on the subject of ‘Primitive Emotional Development’. Rodman's purpose is clear: to convey from the outset the style and flavour of Winnicott the man - his independence of mind, his admitted ‘stealing’ of ideas from others that can only be given back when stamped with the imprint of his own mind; the creative impetus from his not yet openly admitted affair with Clare Britton, later to become his second wife; above all the first signs of his non-compliance with the expectations of the Kleinian circle into which he had been inscribed as a trainee psychoanalyst a decade before and from which he was to spend the next decade painfully extricating himself in search of his own personal and professional identity.

I came to this biography with a sense of keen anticipation. A proper account of Winnicott's life was badly needed and Rodman had already distinguished himself with his capable editing of a selection of Winnicott's letters (Rodman, 1987). I was not too disconcerted by his decision to plunge into the story of Winnicott's life in the middle. Winnicott would have been the first to recognise that an understanding of context was as important for a biography as environment for infancy. And it had the Winnicott stamp of the unexpected.

What did disconcert, however, was the slackness of expression and inaccuracy of detail evident in this opening chapter. To take a couple of examples: Klein, in contrast to Winnicott, did not emphasise ‘the indigenous elements in the conception of the mother in the mind of the child’ (p. 8); she did, though, emphasise the endogenous elements. Winnicott did not ‘speak with a Devon accent’ (p. 4), being very much a metropolitan man, though proud of his Plymouth roots. Of course, these are minor details, but they serve to undermine one's confidence a little.

The origin of this book is outlined in the prologue: a tribute to Donald Meltzer based on a long series of supervisions which have been faithfully portrayed by three founder-members of the Psychoanalytic Group of Barcelona on visits to Dr. Meltzer's home in Oxford between 1993 and 1998. The book is, thus, not written by Meltzer, but his is the main voice which comes through clearly from the 22 clinical presentations which are described in separate chapters. The publication is presented as a debt of gratitude to Meltzer at a point at which the group disbands, and the sense of sadness at ending a mutually rewarding and affectionate encounter is powerfully conveyed.

Chapter headings give date and name of patient together with subheadings such as ‘Incontinence and omnipotence in the world of the infant coming out of the claustrum’, which encompass ideas recognizable from published works. This makes it possible to use the book as reference for dipping into, to gain some view of theory at work in practice, but it also reads well as a whole story and can be read like a novel which is increasingly difficult to put down.

The stories of the patients described, one of whom we follow through on seven different occasions, provide fascinating insights into the particular individuals, but these run parallel with the unfolding of Meltzer's ideas so that by the end of the book it is possible to see that his major concepts have found a place and been elaborated in the process of making sense of complex or obscure material.

Some ideas have not fundamentally changed since The Psycho-analytical Process (Meltzer 1967) which spelt out the concepts of geographical and zonal confusions, emphasizing the crucial role of part objects, which continues to form the basis of Meltzer's approach to interpreting patient's material, well illustrated in this text. Problems of identification and sexual perversions, (Sexual States of Mind, Meltzer 1973) are elaborated, together with aesthetic issues (The Apprehension of Beauty, Meltzer 1988), through to his more recent interest in projective identification as it relates to claustrophobic phenomena (The Claustrum, Meltzer 1992) displaying as always an intense interest in dreams (Dream-Life, Meltzer 1984).

Even in the short time since my paper was published, I am very pleased to say that several people have contacted me pointing out valuable examples of qualitative research undertaken by child psychotherapists that I had failed to refer to - an indication, I think, of how active our profession has already been in the field of research, despite

253

anxieties to the contrary. Mary Boston and Dora Lush have in many respects led the way when it comes to our profession thinking seriously about research and I am very sorry that I did not refer to their ground-breaking work (e.g. Boston, 1989; Boston and Lush, 1994, Lush et al., 1998). Having said that, I do feel the research they describe in these papers has a slightly different methodological basis to the kind of work I was trying to explore (but no less valuable for that), although I agree that their research topic - the finely-tuned, long-term evaluation of psychoanalytic child psychotherapy - falls completely within the second and - to some degree - third circles I described.

Perhaps I should have stressed more clearly that my paper was not intended as a comprehensive review of all the relevant child psychotherapy research already out there; rather, it was a more personal account of some of the material related to qualitative methodology that I had come across during the course of doing my own doctoral research - a journey of discovery that had so excited me I thought it worth sharing with other child psychotherapists who might be thinking about undergoing the rather daunting - and at times isolated - task of engaging in research themselves. In particular, I wanted to draw attention to work taking place slightly outside our own field - by sociologists, adult psychotherapists, family therapists and others - as I imagined that other child psychotherapists were perhaps less likely to have come across these papers.

By sharing with others some of the inspiring work I came across during my rather haphazard journey, I hoped to help them avoid the danger that I am aware I probably fell into, of ‘reinventing the wheel’ when it comes to thinking about how to do clinically-relevant, small-scale research. As I know from my own experience, it is not easy to know where to find the right guidelines. It is perhaps worth pointing out that the otherwise immensely helpful Cumulative Index of the First Forty Years of this Journal (1963-2003), covering over 400 papers, has only one entry under ‘qualitative analysis’ and one under ‘research methodology’ in the Keyword Index (both from the recent themed issue on research, 29/2)! And despite the increasing pressure within our profession to take part in research, the training schools still give very little space to actually including research papers in the curriculum, so that the valuable work that has been done by therapists such as Lush and Boston is too easily neglected - as my own paper demonstrates. I think this is an important issue that needs to be addressed in relation to training and CPD.

Editorial

Janine Sternberg and Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman  

This edition marks a number of changes for the JCP. This is the last issue that occurs within Paul Barrows’ time as senior editor. He is now retiring and the assistant editor, Graham Shulman, steps up to become co-editor. Graham has acted as joint editor on this edition, while Paul remained in the wings to steer us through if necessary. Paul set standards of editorial control, with meticulous attention to detail, that will be hard to match. He devoted much time and energy to the Journal, both to the content of each issue and to its overall direction. However, no editor, no matter how conscientious, can create a journal by himself: we are therefore fortunate to have so much in our work that is well worth writing about, and so many interesting submissions from such a diverse range of authors from which to choose. These will, I hope, enable the JCP to go from strength to strength.

The majority of papers in this edition were written by authors based outside the UK which reflects the international remit and readership of this Journal, but is also, I think, a tribute to the efforts that Paul Barrows has made during his tenure as editor to increase the JCP's links with European authors and publications.

This issue is on the theme of adolescents. The papers published here show child psychotherapists at work with very challenging patients. Adolescent patients are notoriously difficult to engage and keep in regular therapy and it may be that many of those who do ‘stick the course’ are those whose level of disturbance is great. Polmear's article introduces us to some of the fundamental tasks of the adolescent process. She looks at the importance of the adolescent being able to detach him or herself from the parents and shows how this task of separation is linked with the mourning process. Her clinical examples vividly describe some of the ways in which this may go wrong. She highlights the importance of peers and the young person's acceptance by them, and this relationship - or lack of it - with peers is attended to in other papers.

Disturbance of thought, thought as an integrating factor, borderline adolescents, role of the analyst, technical changes,

One of the principal aims of adolescence is the development of the capacity to think for oneself. The authors explore the difficulties caused by disturbances of thinking in borderline adolescents, pointing out the role that the analyst can take in promoting better functioning of their patients’ mental processes. Two cases are explored, one through a supervision and the other through direct clinical experience. Both illustrate the efforts of the analyst to carry out ‘management in the area of thinking’ with those borderline patients who have not received help from their parents to think, and still need to be shown how mentation takes place. The authors propose some changes in technique in order to implement this improvement, including sharing with the patient the way in which the analyst thinks about him. Thinking itself can be an important integrating factor for these patients.

Clinical Commentary

Graham Music and Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman  

Introduction

We are very pleased to introduce our first clinical commentary, a new feature that we hope will appear regularly in the journal and encourage debate and discussion. The idea of course is not new; the British Journal of Psychotherapy, amongst others, has for many years had such a section, and the International Journal of Psychoanalysis has recently introduced a similar format. The idea of critical debate amongst readers is also not new to the JCP; in recent years we have published a lead clinical paper followed by several commentaries on the leading paper (vol. 27, no. 1), and in 1999 we published a symposium on ‘Frustration’ in which three authors (Anne Alvarez, Anne Harrison and Edna O'Shaughnessy) wrote of their different views of this concept.

We hope that these clinical commentaries are within this same spirit of open debate. The format we have used for this issue is that a clinician has anonymously presented a single session as well as some background, and we have asked three senior members of our profession to offer brief commentaries on what they found in the material. In this issue the commentators chosen all have links with different training schools; the aim is not to present ideological views that represent entrenched positions, but rather that discussion and original thinking might be fostered, and we think that this is certainly the case in these commentaries. The format we have used this time is not written in stone and may change, and so feedback would be appreciated, but the overall aim is to maintain a section within the journal in which debate, dialogue and the mutual exchange of ideas can flourish.

The name and background details of the patient have been disguised, and the therapist's name not given, in order to preserve patient confidentiality.

When working in a session, or, as in this case, when reading the clinical report of a session, I pay special attention to the first verbal or non-verbal communication. It is usually a signpost to the underlying unconscious meaning or affect of the later themes. As in dream work, one listens to the manifest content while one searches for the unconscious meaning, especially relating to the transference. In this session there are two initial communications:

The first: ‘She looked smartly dressed and had blue streaks in her hair’. Any unusual change in appearance alerts me to the possibility of the patient's wish to draw attention to an attractive sexual body as a defence against feelings of sexual abnormality or conflict. I am influenced by the knowledge that this is a 16-year-old girl at the height of her adolescent changing body and her relation to it. There must also be a transference message and we are told that Leyla missed the previous five sessions.

The second: Staring at the new blue couch which she sits on, Leyla says, ‘Something has changed in the last 2 weeks’, and ‘It's not as big as the other one’. I hypothesize that she has come to her session full of ambivalence towards her therapist, with thoughts of ending and not needing the therapist any more.

A particularly interesting aspect of this material shows the impact on the psyche of anxieties converging from two sources: the individual domain of adolescence, and the broader global predicament of asylum seekers.

Leyla's family had to flee from their country of origin, and after a period in a refugee camp moved to this country and applied for asylum, which they failed to get. Leyla, who was then 10 and is now 16, has therefore spent her entire adolescence with no secure national status and thus presumably with no real idea of whether, or for how long, she will be allowed to stay here. The threat of a sudden expulsion is not a mere abstraction to her family. On the contrary, it is bound to remain a constant, living fear even if it has been driven into the background by more pressing day to day concerns. In making any comment on this session with Leyla, it is important first of all to take into account the context in which it has occurred and to acknowledge the considerable amount of therapeutic work that has already taken place over a period of 3 years. At the time of referral, Leyla presented a very disturbing clinical picture. She and her family were seen initially for 3 months in family work, followed by individual sessions ‘taken up with the traumatic impact of Leyla's experience’. She continued in individual psychotherapy in varying degrees of intensity. We of course do not know what went on in all of this work but we can imagine the challenge that was set for the therapist in meeting a young adolescent whose dispossessed family had undergone such extraordinarily harsh and frightening experiences of intimidation and humiliation. Questions immediately arise in my mind about the meaning of such experiences for Leyla - what had she witnessed and gone through and what had been left unresolved in her path as a growing young woman in adolescence in this society?

These and other questions cannot be answered through reading this one session, although inevitably I find myself looking for one or two possible clues. To some extent, I find them - for it is possible to gain some sense of Leyla's underlying concerns about loss, impermanence and uncertainty through listening to the therapist's sensitive responses to the material e.g. Leyla's fears of being tricked, ignored, things changing behind her back without her knowing. No doubt, these responses allude to familiar themes worked through in earlier work. Nevertheless, I find it difficult to draw much of a picture from this session of the power of Leyla's past experiences or, more particularly, of her adolescent life. My overall impression of the session is of a piece of therapeutic activity that is part of an ongoing process working well enough within its own momentum but curiously lacking in engagement with the urgency of this young woman's experience in the external world. So much of the work is preoccupied with the subtleties of transference experience. As understandable as this might be, I have to ask myself what is being missed through such singular focus.

‘Does the Professor talk to God?’ So asked Little Hans, child psychotherapy's proto-patient, on hearing Freud's first interpretation addressed directly to him. Of course, Freud was delighted at the child's reaction. But what exactly did it signify? Did the child mean that he had been blest with a heavensent insight about those horses that reared and threatened to bite? Did he just think that his father's friend looked rather like those awesome holy men in the synagogue who used God-talk that little children weren't expected to understand? Or was it because ‘the Professor’ claimed to know the child's past, as well as the future? After all, he had just said:

Long before he was in the world… I had known that a little Hans would come who would be so fond of his mother that he would be bound to feel afraid of his father because of it; and I had told his father this.

(Freud S.E. 10: 42)

I was reminded of the Little Hans episode on reading Eric Rhode's two slim volumes for a number of reasons. Their tone is hieratic, the style lofty, if not quite aloof, creating in the reader a sense of bewilderment or marvel, or a mixture of both, that made me readily identify with the probable sentiments of the young Hans on hearing that first disquisition of Freud. What does he mean? Is what I think he means what he actually means? And if so, how does he know what he professes to know?

Nor is that the only connection. Freud invokes knowledge of a past known yet unknown to his listener; discerning in that past a pattern linking the past thus perceived to present and future. In doing so he speaks like a ‘seer’, believable only on condition of the child himself seeing rightness in his quasi-prophetic perspective. Most of Rhode's readers, I imagine, (at least those who are psychotherapists) will be largely ignorant of the philosophical and other antecedents that he rehearses in the course of his argument. One is invited to accept the past so described as a means of gaining a perspective on the present. The author seems to be aware of, yet comfortable with, the mystification likely to be thus engendered in his readers. This is shown by two allegories that weave their way in and out of these twin volumes. The first emanates from Plato's strange, late dialogue Timaeus (more a monologue, actually) which sets out to present an account of the physical universe and its origins. In doing so it begins with a story, not of how the world, but of how Athens, began. What is significant about this story is the way it starts from, and seeks to explain, the fact that modern Athenians, Socrates included, do not know, ‘have forgotten’ the story of their origins. The mystery of creation, in other words, has to include an explanation of the mystery of why it is mysterious. There is a discontinuity, an interruption between past and present.

This book is not primarily about clinical work, although some psychoanalytical ideas become central to the argument. It is a much more general discussion of the theme in relation to social attitudes toward the phenomenon of incest. I confess I struggled somewhat to apprehend the ‘new perspective’ and how it may differ from established views, but it seems ultimately that the author is arguing for more understanding of the context and meaning of a given act of child abuse than the condemnation which traditionally is applied in the form of legal and social prohibition.

The book consists for the most part of essays each focussing on a particular literary or cinematic depiction of incestuous relationships. However the author sets the scene with a series of autobiographical sketches (which do not include any experience of incest as such). Interspersed also are discussions of ideas from such psychoanalytical writers as Ian Suttie, Sandor Ferenczi, and the more contemporary Valerie Sinason and Estela Well-don. There is also a discussion of the case of James Porter who sexually abused many children in his years as a Catholic priest in the USA.

It is sometimes difficult to know quite how these chapters connect with each other. The autobiographical material leads on to an acknowledgement that in Western Society there is a ‘taboo on tenderness’, in Suttie's phrase. Inhibitions in the expression of affection in attachment relationships may be due to a fear of incestuous impulses. These constraints, leading to isolation and loneliness, are contrasted by the author with the intensity of emotional experience in relatively benign examples of incest. Examples are given in the films Murmur of the Heart, by Louis Malle, and Art for Teachers of Children, by Jennifer Montgomery. In these accounts social convention is thrown over in favour of freedom of expression. However more destructive instances of incest, such as that in the story of Sappho Durrell's suicidal hatred of the father against whom she alleges sexual assault, are not easily integrated in this more permissive view. And the case of James Porter, a predatory paedophile, arouses a very different moral response again. As psychotherapists treating such cases, we quickly learn that there is a world of difference between the occurrence of sex between adult and child in an otherwise loving family, and the sort of victimisation to which a child is subjected in a context of neglect and exploitation.

The author discusses two concepts of transference: the broader use of transference as the ‘total situation ‘, as it was called by Melanie Klein and further elaborated by post-Kleinians, and the narrow use of transference in the traditional sense. Using clinical material from the four-times-a-week analysis of a severely disturbed adolescent over a period of 4 years, the author tries to show how the understanding of the transference as the total situation enabled her to work with this boy who hardly spoke or played. The observation of his non-verbal communication and the counter-transference feelings of the analyst made it possible to formulate hypotheses about the quality of his relationship with the analyst and the inner world of the patient. After the presentation of the clinical material the author points out some misunderstandings of the concept of the total situation in European psychoanalytic discussion.

Conquistador, surgeon, archivist and sculptor; chemist, chess player and jigsaw-puzzle solver; archaeologist, explorer, detective and gambler. These are just some of the identities that Freud offers to describe the role of the psychoanalyst, and which Lydia Flem explores in her wonderful book,

365

Freud the Man. Rather than a purely biographical study, as the title might suggest, this book allows us to peer over Freud's shoulder in the process of writing, to watch him at play ‘with ink, words and paper’ (p. 134), with the spirits of Virgil, Sophocles, Shakespeare and - above all - Goethe hovering about him. As the original French title, L'homme Freud, suggests, this book is closer in mood to the imaginative explorations of Freud's own L'homme Moses (re-titled in English as Moses and Monotheism] than to the more straightforwardly biographical works of Ernest Jones or Peter Gay.

In each of the 10 chapters Flem voyages around different metaphorical configurations found in Freud's work, discovering ‘an infinite kaleidoscope of figurative expressions, comparisons and analogies’ (p. 169) that permeate Freud's writings. Because the patterns are always changing, Flem argues, Freud ‘never offers the reader a conclusive, dogmatic text but instead an always open construction site, research in progress, thinking as it is being thought, and he invites his reader to accompany him step by step, in vivo’ (p. 169). We might say that the reader is asked to follow Freud on an ‘imaginary walk’, to borrow the phrase that Freud used to describe the shape of The Interpretation of Dreams. The structure of this book, as Freud acknowledged in a letter to Wilhelm Fliess, was taken not from traditional academic theses, but from Dante's Divine Comedy, with the hero first lost in a dark wood (previous theories of dreams) before being led, gradually but surely, towards the light of true understanding.

Flem suggests that the experience the reader of Freud's work is asked to go through mirrors the process of an analysis itself, ‘from shadow to clarity, from the unknown towards a new knowledge’ (p. 107). But it is also Freud's own self-professed method of composition, a method inspired by an essay called ‘The Art of Becoming an Original Writer in Three Days’ (which Freud received for his 13th birthday and kept until the end of his life): to ‘throw oneself into a line of thought and to follow it wherever it leads’ (p. 111).

This admirable and refreshing series sets out to present psychoanalytic theories and

126

concepts in a way that is accessible and meaningful to the interested reader. The authors are each rooted in a psychoanalytic perspective but with a range of different experiences including: work across the age range in both NHS settings and private practice, teaching, writing, and non-clinical work. There are 17 books at present, each taking up a particular theme significant in psychoanalytic thinking. I have selected a few to provide a snapshot of the series which I hope conveys my experience of an enjoyable, interesting and generally refreshing look at a range of significant issues. For example: Guilt, Depression, The Unconscious, Phantasy, Anxiety.

It would be all too easy to quickly become caught up in the complexity of any single theme, daunted by differing theoretical models and the potentially wide audience including peers. The authors each pursue their task and in the main successfully manage to maintain their position of authority in relation to psychoanalytic ideas whilst locating them firmly in the ordinary, everyday experiences that resonate with a wide readership and enrich psychoanalytic understanding.

The topics were approached differently, reflecting the diversity amongst the authors. In the short introduction to Depression, Jeremy Holmes immediately and adroitly draws the reader into the familiarity of experience as well as informing the reader about depression. He writes: ‘Most of the time most of us feel mostly OK. We can sleep in our beds at night; our appetites - gustatory, sexual and exploratory - function normally; we can concentrate on whatever we happen to be doing, make plans, cope with setbacks and expect that things will turn out all right. … For the depressed person, none of these simple securities can be taken for granted …’ (p. 3). Holmes continues to unveil the complexity of depression emphasising the significance of loss in the genesis of this condition.

Editorial

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

This is the last Editorial that I shall be writing, as my term of office ends in December 2004, and the next issue of the Journal will be largely produced by my co-editor and assistant editor, prior to them taking over full responsibility.

In many ways it is a particularly fitting number to have as my swan-song. It begins with a paper by my dear colleague and former co-editor, Hamish Canham, who died so tragically young and who would have been such an excellent editor of the Journal. He was also, of course, a particularly gifted clinician who was very committed to working with children who had suffered severe deprivation. This paper, originally given at an annual conference of the Association of Child Psychotherapists, is a fine example of his work and shows his patience, firmness and resilience in the face of a very difficult patient. It is the kind of patient that will be familiar to many child psychotherapists and Canham's paper will be greatly welcomed by those struggling with such cases.

I am also very pleased to be able to publish the next paper by Palacio-Espasa. In part because we have not previously featured his work although he has published very widely elsewhere, but also because of my own particular interest in parent - infant work. The present article was in fact held over from our Under-Fives edition because of shortage of space in that number. It also reflects the continuing development of the Journal's links with European colleagues, evidenced by an increasing number of papers from that area.

The growing international scope of the Journal is again a feature of the papers that follow. These are drawn from our 40th Birthday Conference which was generously sponsored by the publishers. It was a very successful and friendly event that prompted lively discussion and a thought-provoking exchange of views, and those who were unable to attend can now have the pleasure of reading the four presentations that we enjoyed. The first paper by Miller looks at the Journal ‘Then and Now’, placing it in its historical context and giving an overview of developments in child psychotherapy over the last 40 years. We also solicited papers to reflect the broader international context of child psychotherapy, with contributions from America, Australia and Europe. In the best tradition of the Journal, these are largely clinical papers and they give a vivid account of the profession across the globe. As Miller shows, the clinical preoccupations that they exemplify have been features of the Journal throughout its existence.

Letter to the editors from Mary Boston

Dear Editors

We were interested in the paper by Nicholas Midgley in the last issue of the Journal, ‘Sailing between Scylla and Charybdis: Incorporating qualitative approaches into child psychotherapy research’. We certainly agree that the way forward in such research is the more systematic use of qualitative methods as we stressed in our earlier five papers, published in this and other journals.

We were therefore surprised at his statement (p. 93) ‘To my knowledge virtually no child psychotherapists have, up till now, published research making explicit use of qualitative methodologies.’ He adds in a note that there are two such papers deriving from the Tavistock clinical doctorate programme, though some have not yet been published.

There are also several published qualitative research studies by child psychotherapists in books as well as journals, for example on adopted and looked-after children, psychotic and autistic children, eating disorders, sexually abused girls and boy abusers. These, including our own study of adopted and looked after children in psychotherapy, have in common the more systematic use of qualitative methods on a number of cases with the aim of generating new knowledge and further hypotheses. Surely these would come into at least Midgley's ‘second’ circle and some the third. May we respectfully suggest that Midgley researches his references more thoroughly, in spite of his impressive bibliography list.

Editorial

Janine Sternberg and Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

This edition of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy contains an interesting collection of papers which show a number of the areas that child psychotherapists are preoccupied with at the moment. We see the characteristic of thoughtful professional work, with practice influencing theory, and problems in the consulting room leading the clinicians to revise their theories. We can note the way the authors often start from their individual experiences in the consulting room, and struggle with and muse about the impact of the child or the family on themselves. They then, over time, think further and more deeply about what has been going on, creating possible new ways of understanding both their experience, and how that experience relates to previous theories. For these clinicians this process has culminated in the papers which we are now able to read, many of which extend already accepted theoretical concepts.

In her paper Rhode shows just this mix of detailed clinical work and advances in theory. Although Rhode's paper arises out of her work with a particular patient population, the ideas within it can be extended to work with others. The impact of trauma is apparent here, as it is in the papers by Jackson and Emanuel. Rhode takes her ideas about the geometry of the mouth and nipple, and parallels this idea of the perpendicular with the nature of the paternal influence. This most interesting idea about the quality of the perpendicular and the bringing together, or not, of the maternal and paternal can also be seen in other papers in this volume where the role of the father, including the impact of father's absence, is examined closely.

Music's paper challenges some of our assumptions about what is implied by the terms ‘maternal’ and ‘paternal’, and delineates how thoughts about these issues can influence our clinical practice. He disputes the traditional view that the father rescues the child from an over-close entanglement with the mother. He shows how maternal and paternal characteristics may be seen in the consulting room, and how the therapist's awareness of the stance they are adopting is essential to the success of the therapeutic encounter. The importance of the maternal and paternal stance, and the child's separate place, together with the creation of a family unit are evident in Miller's paper about work with parents. She highlights the importance of oedipal and transgenerational issues in this work, noting how the parents’ inability to negotiate ‘the essential ambiguities’ of the Oedipal situation have enormous repercussions on their capacities to manage many aspects of ordinary parenting. She offers her thoughts in an easy, effortless style that could mask the sophistication of the thinking about this actually very complex process.

Nicholas Midgley   Child psychotherapist at the Marlborough Family Service and the Royal Free Hospital, London, and an editor of the Bulletin of the Association of Child Psychotherapists. At the Anna Freud Centre he co-ordinates a number of qualitative research projects and is Course Tutor in Psychoanalytic Theory for the M.Sc. in Psychoanalytic Developmental Psychology. He has recently completed a clinical doctorate at University College London on the long-term follow-up of child psychoanalysis.
Psychoanalytic research; qualitative methodology; research-practice gap; evidence based practice; therapy process and outcome.

Starting from the acknowledged gap between research and practice in child psychotherapy, this paper offers an historical perspective on the relation between these two activities, and suggests that qualitative approaches to research may offer new ways of bringing them together. After introducing the fundamental concepts of qualitative analysis, three areas where qualitative forms of research may be useful to child psychotherapists are explored: relevant but non-psychotherapy research; accounts of therapy research; and therapy process research. Examples of all of these types of research are presented, and some of the challenges to incorporating qualitative approaches into child psychotherapy research are discussed.

This volume, the third in the Cassel Hospital Monograph series, is dedicated to the work with children and adolescents and brings together a number of papers, some amended versions of ones that have been previously published. This may account for the repetitious description of this unique institution; some judicious editing with a general preface describing the setting could have been helpful.

The Cassel is one of a small number of specialist hospitals within the National Health Service offering in-patient treatment for people with severe personality disorders. It has a long tradition of combining psychosocial nursing and psychoanalytic psychotherapy within a therapeutic community.

An extremely clear introduction by Lesley Day gives an overview of the work of the hospital with a summary of each chapter. This work is very helpfully set in the context of the provision (or rather lack of provision) of mental health services for children and adolescents and their parents in the NHS. The title of the book reflects the reality of these patients’ less than favourable experiences and the life histories described make uncomfortable reading. The authors describe the way in which patients internalized their experiences, and how these unfolded during their stay in the hospital, in a setting which offered a structured and containing environment. More often than not, the patients’ life experiences were re-enacted in the relationship to therapist and nurse as well as the wider community, and the book explores to what extent these experiences could be worked through and modified during the course of their treatment.

The majority of the papers are clinical accounts of treatment of the most disturbed and disturbing patients e.g. those with Munchausen syndrome by proxy, and borderline adolescents.

The title encompasses the central dilemma; the perpetrator-youngster is a perpetrator,

249

but views himself as victim. This is elaborated in the first chapter, which gives a clear overview of the subject. Compulsion, rigidity and the presence of aggression in sexuality are described as pathognomonic of perversion. Woods argues that the subjective meaning of abuse determines whether the abused child becomes abusive. The complex reactions elicited in the therapist by the abuser/abused are highlighted, as well as the challenges of using countertransference constructively, while walking the technical tightrope of combining the duality of victim and perpetrator.

Chapter 2 discusses psychotherapy in a systemic context. This is a candid and comprehensive appraisal of factors - including professional rivalries and anxieties - that divide mental health professionals, ultimately diminishing their effectiveness. Woods believes that cooperation amongst professionals - who maintain differentiated roles - maximizes the possibility for a successful treatment. Apart from making use of transference and countertransference, the therapist offers a different emotional experience to the youngster by being a real and ‘new object’ (A Freud, 1966, p. 38). The author refers to Bentovim's paper ‘Trauma Organised Systems’ which emphasises the network of factors, including fear, dependence, blame and denial, that interact reciprocally to facilitate and perpetuate abuse. While this conceptual framework seems illuminating to understanding the internal world of the abused/abuser, the schematic diagram included is rather confusing. It was unclear to me whether the lines with arrowheads were to be understood as vectors (having magnitude, direction and causality) or whether they indicated characteristics of an element in the diagram.

Chapter 3 uses illustrative vignettes to highlight some common themes in therapeutic work with abused/abusers. The clear discussion enables the reader to gain insight into the ways of relating that are particular to these youngsters, and that constitute additional challenges to the therapist. These include the abused/abuser's tendency to deny and attack, to attempt to sexualize the therapeutic relationship, and to re-enact rather than describe experiences. The boundaries of the therapeutic relationship are particularly challenged by the concerns about child protection, inevitably aroused by these youngsters. The author argues that by expressing concerns about the child's safety outside the therapy room, the therapist mitigates the potential perversion of the therapeutic relationship from confidentiality to a secrecy that allows the perpetuation of abuse.

Those of us who have elected to spend our days exploring psychic reality have a conundrum to deal with: how ‘internal’ is the internal world? Just how do the thoughts, fantasies, images and beliefs populating the mind get there, and take the form that they do? If, as Chris Oakley (1989) has suggested, our habitual assumption that the psyche is located inside the skull has led to partial sightedness and error, what alternative sites for the location of personal suffering might there be? Oakley resituates psychoanalytic accounts of psychic reality in what he calls ‘the space of the between’. From this perspective, defence mechanisms take place between us, in language. The unconscious may well be inside us, but it is equally true that we are in unconsciousness. In adopting this frame, whilst exploring individual, idiosyncratic formations, we are inevitably simultaneously exploring cultural dynamics. For those who like to believe in a straightforwardly apolitical clinical realm, it may come as something of an unwelcome surprise to find that there is no ‘politics-free zone’ in psychic life - we not only grow up in culture, but it is part of our nature as human creatures to have culture ‘inbuilt’, as it were, as an essential component of our being. The psyche, in this sense, is reminiscent of sport during South Africa's apartheid regime: politics has not been dragged in by a few mischievous Leftists - it has always been there. As Farhad Dalal puts it in this courageous, rigorous book on racism, ‘the structures of society are reflected in the structures of the psyche, and if the first of these is colour coded, then so will be the second.’ (p. 7).

We do not need to imagine a viciously racist regime such as the apartheid system to explore racism: Dalal exquisitely deconstructs complacent liberal assumptions by showing us, in black and white, as it were, just how ubiquitous it is in our supposedly post-political liberal-democratic world (including that minute part of it called the consulting room). It can hardly be otherwise, for it is part of Dalal's disquietingly convincing quest to show just how deeply sedimented it is in the very language we use to describe and, unavoidably, construct, one another. Language may be something we prefer to think of as a tool kit we use to make meaningful contact with each other, and Richard Rorty (1989), amongst others, has argued elegantly for just this conceptualization. But, as Lacan (1956) in particular knew well, language also uses us - a humiliating realization for anyone who still wishes to believe that the ego is master in its own house.

Parent - infant therapy, parental narcissism, brief therapy, parenthood, pre-transference,

In this article the author discusses some of the indications for short- or long-term parent- infant psychotherapeutic interventions in terms of what he defines as ‘problems of parenthood’ and ‘problems of parental narcissism’. Brief parent—infant psychotherapeutic interventions are most frequently indicated in the case of the former: more neurotic problems of parenthood where the parents present a manic or counter-depressive type of narcissism. Masochistic problems of parenthood are also susceptible to treatment through brief parent- infant interventions, although in such cases treatment may have to be continued in another modality of long-term psychotherapy. More dissociated problems of parental narcissism constitute a contraindication for brief psychotherapeutic parent—infant interventions. The persecutory narcissism of these parents contributes to a ‘negative pre-transference’ which creates a major resistance to the therapeutic process.

In work with couples where there is a child referred to a Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service, there are opportunities to observe and to work with unresolved Oedipal issues brought by the parents to the task of creating a family. This fascinating book introduces, with many clinical highlights, the innovative psychoanalytic work with toddlers and their families which started at the Tavistock Clinic in the early 1980s, known as the ‘Under Fives’ Counselling Service’. Lisa Miller, a pioneer and very experienced child psychotherapist in this kind of brief work, describes in her Foreword how ‘the families arrive in pain and anxiety, pushed to enact internal states, taken over by forces they feel they cannot control either in the child or parents’ reactions to it. They don't know why they are behaving as they would not wish to behave. It is plain that powerful and complex understanding can take place in this brief work. Simply by coming the family announces its readiness to seek help and it is of the utmost importance that the families are seen without delay.’ This book is one of the contributions of child psychotherapists from the Tavistock Clinic in London to parent - infant psychotherapy. One can trace in it the theoretical influences of the work of Klein, Bion, Winnicott, brief psychodynamic psychotherapy, parent - infant psychotherapy, attachment theory, the family therapy work of Byng-Hall, and recent developments in the neurosciences. This book is a very welcome and important addition to the forum of infant - parent work, although its main focus is on work with toddlers and their families.

The first part of Pozzi's book covers theoretical ideas and technical aspects of short term and focused psychoanalytic counselling where young children are seen together with their parents and siblings in what ever combination they wish to be seen. The Tavistock model of infant observation is dealt with in a separate chapter, emphasizing its ever-increasing importance. The second part of the book consists of rich case histories.

The book covers the most common complaints and symptoms met in under fives’ counselling. These are dealt with in different chapters, including: eating problems, sleeping problems, separation problems and how these get entangled with parental difficulties, soiling, bereavement and loss, learning disabilities, borderline children, hyperactivity and - not so often written about - gender identity. Postnatal depression, so common but often undetected, and mental illness in the family are important chapters. These topics are dealt with very vividly and make for exciting reading.

Transference on to the container; infantile transference; infantile autism; psychic bisexuality; ‘nest of babies’ fantasy.

Starting from Frances Tustin's description of failure of the containing function in autistic children due to a splitting between the masculine and feminine aspects of the containing object, the author suggests that the first stage in the psychoanalytic treatment of an autistic child consists in restoring that function by working through what he calls the transference on to the container. His description of container bisexuality differs slightly from that given by Tustin. In the author's description, the masculine elements of the container do not penetrate the female ones, but rather strengthen them in the same way as buttresses strengthen a building. Once the transference on to the container is sufficiently worked through, the child can begin to trust the containing capacities of the object. Thereafter, an infantile transference, as defined by Melanie Klein, begins to develop. That transference tends to have a special intensity in autistic children, with the emergence of a fantasy that Tustin called the ‘nest of babies’ fantasy. A clinical illustration of that fantasy is given. The infantile transference represents the second stage in the psychoanalytic treatment of an autistic child. The third stage consists in working through the transference neurosis as described by Freud. An autistic child who reaches this degree of psychic organization may look like an ordinary child, but this level of mental functioning will remain very unstable for some time. The end of the treatment can be envisaged when the child continues to make progress mentally even during breaks in the analysis. Clinical material illustrates the three stages described in the paper.

In this paper I shall describe the psychotherapeutic treatment of a 14-year-old boy, who suffered from mild Asperger's syndrome. This adolescent had a multiplicity of imaginary friends, which protected him from catastrophic feelings of loneliness and deadness, but at the same time interfered with the possibility of establishing meaningful relations with human beings. As the relationship with the therapist gradually gained the vitality and importance originally invested in his parallel fantasy world, the imaginary companions simultaneously faded away. His imagination then became more closely connected to inner reality and to creative processes. The psychoanalytic literature on imaginary companions is reviewed, and it is suggested that the concept of a self-protective device could be usefully applied to understanding the functions that this fantasy performed for the patient.

Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham

London

Hamish Canham   Was a Consultant Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic where he played a key role as Joint Organizing Tutor and Academic Tutor on the child psychotherapy training. He was also Joint Organising Tutor for the Course ‘Working with Groups in the Public and Independent Sectors’. He taught on the Tavistock-model child psychotherapy training in Bologna, Italy and was Joint Editor of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy 2001 -2003. He died in July 2003.
Counter-transference; technique; abuse; deprivation; violence.

The technical difficulties posed for the child psychotherapist working with children who have themselves experienced violence and abuse are addressed. A distinction is drawn between violence in the service of communicating about such experiences and violence that arises from more perverse aspects of the patient. The therapist's need to pay close attention to his counter-transference is emphasized. From an example of a single session we see the therapist's struggle to receive the communicative aspects of extreme acting-out behaviour at the same time as creating a safe setting in which thinking can take place.

Ricky Emanuel   Head of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy Services, Royal Free Hospital, Camden and Islington Mental Health and Social Care Trust, and Clinical Lead, Camden CAMHS, Camden PCT. He teaches at the Tavistock Clinic, London, the Birmingham Trust for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and abroad in Italy and Turkey. He has a long-standing interest in neuroscience and psychoanalysis, having worked in Artificial Intelligence in the 1970s before training as a child psychotherapist. This is of particular relevance to his liaison work in a hospital setting involving developmental paediatrics.
Neuroscience, child psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, trauma, emotional regulation, emotion, feeling, persecutory superego,

This paper suggests that some neuroscience concepts particularly concerned with brain pathways in trauma and fear, as well as the neurobiology of emotion, provide an additional vertex to the psychoanalytic understanding of patients’ material. The role of the body has been neglected in psychoanalytic thought and formulations in favour of purely ‘mental’ experience. The paper attempts to show how neuro-psychoanalytic understanding, which is conveyed to patients through interpretation, can increase their depth of understanding. Different types of memory are delineated and the paper describes a simplified schema of emotional processing, drawing on Damasio's distinction between emotion as an instinctual body based experience and its mental representation as feeling. Clinical examples are used to illustrate the usefulness of the distinction. The concept of emotional regulation is discussed as well as showing how its failure is associated with the appearance of persecutory superego structures.

Emil Jackson   Child and adolescent psychotherapist working at the Tavistock Clinic and Brent Centre for Young People. He is associate organising tutor for the course on ‘Working with Groups in the Public and Independent Sector’ and also teaches on the Child Psychotherapy training and the MA in Psychoanalytic Observational Studies at the Tavistock Clinic.
Play, technique, adoption, resilience, hope,

In this paper, I describe the first 2 years of intensive psychotherapy of a multiply traumatized 5-year-old girl. I explore some of the ways in which violent and traumatic experiences were re-lived in the therapy and how they impacted on both patient and therapist. Within the discussion and illustrated by clinical vignettes, I consider the importance of play, not only as a vehicle for symbolic communication or as a means of re-playing and re-working internal object relationships, but also as the arena in which new experiences can be forged into internal reality, often for the first time. I also hope to raise for further consideration questions about the complex and disturbing experiences, pressures and technical dilemmas that are frequently encountered in such work.

Ambivalence; ego ideal; identification; pseudo ego ideal; superego in adolescence.

The author reviews the main points in Freud's 1917 paper ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ and relates them to the process of both normal and troubled adolescent development. Using clinical examples she illustrates the ways in which the processes Freud describes in melancholia operate in some disturbed adolescents such that instead of mourning the lost objects of their childhood, they become stuck, remaining ambivalently attached to them and incorporating them into their final adult identity and sexual organization.

Margaret Cohen's book is essentially about people's stories: the heartfelt telling and listening of lives shared in a community of nurses, doctors, mothers and fathers and their tiny, vulnerable and sometimes very sick babies. ‘In some sense I feel that my whole life is poured into this book’ she says in her Introduction to the telling of her stories from the 12 years she worked in Neonatal Intensive Care. Beginning with some personal recollections, her memories of a childhood, wartime in Kent, a kitchen garden and her father's ‘huge and competent hands’, the reader is drawn into the very heart of the matter, that the work of the child psychotherapist in a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) resonates with the intimate and private beginnings and endings in our own lives and how deeply personal and subjective experiences weave themselves into the ways in which we work in this medical domain. In this beautifully written book, Cohen's hugely competent heart and mind has given child psychotherapists, and other professionals working in this field, a real gift.

What lies at the centre of NICU life are the babies and it is their experience which the child psychotherapist, using psychoanalytically informed infant observation, attempts to articulate and render meaningful. To this Cohen blends her knowledge of philosophical issues to consider the inexhaustible interpretations of the experience of these fragile and traumatised infants, and the states of mind evoked in their parents and carers, by their dramatic entry into the world.

Thus the door of the first chapter opens into the secluded, awesomely technical world of the NICU, riven on occasion by ways of working which do not always sit comfortably together, and this is elaborated in the chapter ‘Two ways of seeing’. An encounter with a frail baby of 24 weeks gestational age introduces the first narrative, which, as well as being one of several fine examples of infant observation in the book, also draws attention to the dilemma of perspective, ‘two different ways of seeing the same things’ (p. 10). All of us working at the bed-side/cot-side in this applied hospital setting, with its emphasis on rational thought and practical activity, will be familiar with this kind of struggle to find a place for imagination and the irrational, not only in our interpretations of baby observations but also in our attempts to elucidate the perspective of the medical and nursing teams as well as that of the parents.

It was with great enthusiasm that we received Dr. Britton's latest book. After making note of the dedication: ‘To Ritaclare, who has put up with the author of the last chapter of this book for many years,’ the reading took a radical turn (to the last chapter of the book, of course). In this chapter on ‘the narcissistic problem of sharing space’ the reader finds not only the qualities of creativity, lucidity and originality that have characterized Britton's previous writings, but also the ordinary and open humanity that is the hallmark of Britton the man.

Britton writes, ‘One thing in common between living with someone and being in analysis is the problem of sharing thoughts and sharing space’ (p. 166). Britton's book had already evoked this dilemma from the moment it arrived in the mail. With two analysts in the house - one of us also a child analyst - we decided to take turns reading the book, sharing our thoughts and the space of this review.

Beneath Britton's intriguing title, the reader witnesses the product of many years of psychoanalytic experience with both children and adults. This experience has clearly fanned out and permeated Britton's thinking about literature and social phenomena, thinking that has surely reverberated in his continued practice and teaching of analysis, further enriching and refining his clinical work in turn. In this book the reader encounters an author who is able to make room for scholarship and for heart, discipline and genuine passion that invites the reader to join him on a voyage of reconsideration and fresh evaluation of psychoanalytic-diagnostic concepts, metapsychological constructs and related clinical issues.

As a major proponent of post-Kleinian psychoanalytic thinking in London, the author reliably provides case vignettes from his own practice to illustrate his ideas and arguments, sparing the reader the broad generalizations of abstract philosophical discourse that can be examined only by criteria of internal and external consistency. Britton is first and foremost an astute and sensitive clinician. Whether or not one subscribes to the Kleinian foundations of his approach, there can be no doubt that he is a committed and reflective analyst. To commemorate the 40th year of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy the current Editor, Paul Barrows, has compiled a selection of notable papers to represent the creative work of the Journal from its beginnings up to the 1980s. Another collection will probably follow representing later texts of importance that may well owe their origins and inspiration to these earlier papers. This year also marks the release by the publisher of the first Cumulative Index - another indispensable aid to surveying the history of the Journal.

The criteria for choosing these ‘key’ papers were (a) their inaccessibility to a contemporary readership due to the absence of back copies or having not been reprinted elsewhere (b) the frequency with which a text has been cited for teaching and learning purposes, and of course (c) their being distinguished contributions in their own right.

As the Editor states, such a commemorative edition not only celebrates the international success of the Journal today but also the growth in the profession of child psychotherapy itself.

The book is divided into three sections covering theoretical, clinical and applied contributions. There is a general introduction and, in addition, each section begins with its own introduction by the Editor that reviews the chapters so thoughtfully and comprehensively as to make the job of the reviewer almost unnecessary. However the Editor raises several interesting issues for the reader to ponder and one of these is the observation that nowadays there is a greater convergence between different theoretical schools of child psychotherapy concerning certain aspects of their work.

I would like to shape my review around this subject as it bears directly on some of the papers chosen and on the historical dimension to the life of the Journal itself. The Journal first appeared at a time when conceptual and technical differences between Anna Freudian and Kleinian ‘schools’ of child analysis in Britain were starkly drawn. Both ‘schools’ were making pioneering statements about child mental health issues yet there existed between them a degree of mutual disagreement at times bordering on strategic misunderstanding. This grew logically out of the feud between Anna Freud and Melanie Klein in the British Psychoanalytic Society (1941-1945) that became known as the ‘Controversial Discussions’. In this feud both sides had failed to convince each other of their viewpoints, but at least they had marked out their territory with some degree of precision and coherence. In the child sphere, differences were set aside during the successful formation of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (non-Medical) in 1949, but with the founding of a new Journal several years later each side would find it difficult to resist using it as a vehicle for buttressing differences over developmental theory and technique.
